DETROIT, Michigan (CNN) -- It's a stimulus plan on sneakers. The NCAA men's Final Four at Detroit's Ford Field could generate $30 million to $50 million from visitors. The NCAA men's basketball Final Four couldn't come at a better time for the city of Detroit -- the hard-hit capital of the U.S. auto industry at the center of the state of Michigan's economic woes. The 12-percent unemployment rate here is the highest in the nation, and with the Big Three automakers all needing multibillion-dollar government bailouts in an attempt to stay afloat, the future isn't much brighter, some say. "We need some help," said Detroit resident Mark Franklin, who took his 5-year-old son to Friday's Hershey's College All-Star Game at Ford Field. "There are too many people out of work already. Even if you have a job, you know someone who doesn't." Enter the Final Four and a quartet of powerhouse college basketball teams -- all seeking NCAA brass. Connecticut, Michigan State, North Carolina and Villanova have won a combined nine NCAA championships and reached 31 Final Fours. But more important to the city are the visitors -- and the wallets -- that college basketball's marquee weekend will bring to Detroit. City leaders expect 100,000 fans to visit -- staying in hotel rooms, renting cars and spending an anticipated $30 million to $50 million. The participation of Michigan State adds icing on the cake. The school's campus sits just 90 miles away, in East Lansing, giving the Spartans a home-floor advantage as they give locals some added pride on a special weekend. MSU helped things along mightily by advancing to the finals Saturday, defeating Connecticut 82-73. In the national championship game, the Spartans will play North Carolina, 83-69 victors over Villanova later Saturday. More than half the Michigan State players are from in-state and many have felt the impact of the region's economic woes. "I have family that are unemployed right now," said sophomore guard Durrell Summers, who starred at Detroit's Redford Covenant High School. "[For the Final Four] to bring that kind of money in, hopefully it can help open up jobs for my family and for other families because some people got laid off for no reason." Watch Elaine Quijano's report on a GM dealer's perspective . Detroit's first Final Four is the latest in a series of big sporting events for the city. The Pistons have hosted a pair of NBA Finals in suburban Auburn Hills, while the NHL's Red Wings have won two Stanley Cups at downtown Joe Louis Arena. Baseball's Tigers have played in a World Series and its home, Comerica Park, hosted an MLB All-Star game. This weekend's host venue, Ford Field, was the site of Super Bowl XL and Oakland Hills Country Club was home to the 2004 Ryder Cup and the PGA Championship last August in nearby Bloomfield Hills. This is the first year of a new stadium configuration for the Final Four, requiring host domes to use all permanent seating to meet a 70,000-seat minimum. "You see people driving up just to take a picture of the Final Four sign on (Ford Field). It's something to be proud of," Franklin said. "Now we need city leaders to take advantage of it."

# Final Four Offers Glimmer of Hope for Economically Battered Detroit

**DETROIT** — As the nation's economic crisis continues to hammer the Motor City, local officials and business owners are pinning their hopes on an unlikely source of relief: the 2009 NCAA men's Final Four basketball tournament.

The event, held at Ford Field, is expected to draw tens of thousands of visitors to a city struggling with soaring unemployment and the near-collapse of the American auto industry. For a metropolitan area battered by plant closures and foreclosures, the influx of tourists represents a rare bright spot.

"We need this. The whole city needs this," said Marcus Freeman, who owns a small restaurant near downtown. "The last few months have been brutal. When people come in for the games, they eat, they buy, they spend money. That keeps my doors open and keeps my people working."

## An Economic Lifeline

Local tourism officials estimate the tournament could generate significant revenue for hotels, restaurants, and retailers throughout the region. With Detroit's unemployment rate among the highest in the nation, every dollar spent by visiting fans carries added weight.

"Events like this remind everyone that Detroit is still standing, still fighting," said Angela Whitfield, a downtown hotel employee. "For a few days, the focus is on basketball and not on all the bad news. That means a lot to the people who live here."

City leaders hope the national spotlight will do more than fill hotel rooms — they want it to reshape perceptions of a city too often defined by its economic troubles.

## Players Weigh In

The athletes competing for the national championship acknowledged the significance of playing in a city facing such hardship.

"You can feel that the community is really behind this," one Final Four player told reporters. "It's cool to think that us being here, playing the game we love, might help the people here even a little bit. That's bigger than basketball."

Another player added, "Everywhere we go, people are thanking us for coming. You don't always get that. It makes you want to give them a great show."

## Cautious Optimism

While the tournament offers a welcome boost, some residents remain realistic about its limits.

"It's a weekend. It's not going to fix everything," said longtime Detroit resident Carla Jennings. "But you take what you can get. Right now, a little hope goes a long way around here."

For a city hungry for good news, the roar of the crowds at Ford Field may provide exactly that — even if only for one memorable weekend.

**DETROIT** — On the floor of Ford Field, where the Detroit Lions spend autumn Sundays absorbing the city's frustration, a basketball court has been laid down at the center of a football cathedral. Around it, workers unspooled miles of cable, hoisted video boards toward the rafters and arranged upwards of 70,000 seats for a game meant for a room a fraction of the size.

For four days this spring, college basketball's Final Four belongs to a city that could use the distraction.

But the men and women bolting down bleachers and testing the sound system carry a knowledge that no visiting fan or television crew can share. Outside these walls, the region that built the American century is coming apart. The automakers whose names once meant permanence — General Motors, Chrysler, Ford — are fighting for survival on federal life support. Michigan's unemployment rate leads the nation, hovering above 12 percent, and in some neighborhoods here it climbs far higher than the official count admits. Every empty storefront on Woodward Avenue tells the story the brackets cannot.

"You want to be proud of your city," said one arena worker, a temporary hire who lost a job on an auto-parts line eighteen months ago and would give only his first name, Marcus. "But pride doesn't pay the mortgage. This," he said, gesturing at the rising grandstands, "this is a paycheck for a couple weeks. Then what?"

That question hangs over Detroit's improbable turn in the national spotlight.

The NCAA awarded this Final Four to Ford Field years ago, when the arithmetic was about attendance records, not survival. A domed stadium meant the tournament could sell more tickets to a single game than any building had before. Nobody in the planning meetings imagined that the event would arrive as the domestic auto industry teetered on the edge of collapse, or that the host city would become shorthand, in headlines from coast to coast, for economic ruin.

Now the coincidence feels almost cruel, and almost redemptive.

City officials talk about the estimated economic impact — tens of millions of dollars flowing into hotels, restaurants and bars that have watched their regulars vanish along with the assembly-line shifts. The convention center has hangers-on hoping the crowds will remember there is a downtown worth returning to. Restaurateurs who trimmed their staffs to the bone are calling laid-off waiters back, if only for the weekend.

"We'll take whatever we can get," said a manager at a bar within walking distance of the stadium, where the lunch crowd has thinned to a handful of regulars nursing drafts. "One good weekend won't fix anything. But it reminds people we're still here."

The teams themselves, four of them chasing a national championship, arrive largely insulated from all this — young men focused on scouting reports and shooting drills, staying in downtown hotels, bused to a stadium and back. Their coaches speak the practiced language of one-game-at-a-time. For them, Detroit is a venue, a stage, a line on a résumé.

Yet basketball has always been the game of hard places, of playgrounds and gymnasiums in cities the prosperity forgot. There is a fitness, maybe, in bringing its grandest weekend to a town that knows something about pressing on when the odds turn ugly. Detroit does not need to be told about resilience. It has been practicing the art for decades, long before the current crisis, in a slow erosion of population and payrolls that predates any bailout debate.

The autoworkers who once packed Tiger Stadium and cheered the Pistons through their "Bad Boys" championships understood the compact: the plants provided the wages, and the wages provided the tickets, and the teams provided the release. That compact is now broken, or at least badly bent. When these fans look at the Final Four, some see a party they can no longer afford, a $150 seat in a stadium built by an industry laying them off.

Still, they will watch. Televisions will glow in living rooms across the metro area, tuned to a game happening a few miles away and a world apart. And for a few hours, the score that matters will be the one on the board, not the one on the unemployment rolls.

Outside Ford Field, the wind off the river cuts cold, and the skyline shows its gaps like a smile missing teeth. Inside, the court is ready, the nets are hung, and a city waits to remember what it feels like to host something the whole country wants to see.

"Maybe people watch and they think, that's Detroit, that's not so bad," Marcus said, pulling his jacket tighter as his shift ended and the real Detroit reclaimed him. "Maybe they buy a car. I don't know. I just know I've got work till Monday."

Then the tournament will pack up its cables and bleachers and move on, as tournaments do, leaving behind a city that has learned, more than most, how to carry on after the crowd goes home.
